# ECG Means

> Independent, clinician-reviewed plain-English explanations of the phrases printed on ECG/EKG reports. Every page is written and reviewed by Dr. Faisal Irshad, MBBS (PMDC 54440-S) and states plainly whether a finding is usually harmless, context-dependent, needs clinician review, or warrants prompt care. Educational only; not a substitute for the clinician who ordered the test.

## ECG Report Phrases
- [ECG Report Phrases Explained](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-report-phrases/): The wording the machine prints — abnormal ECG, borderline ECG, septal infarct, nonspecific T wave abnormality — and what each line really means.
- [Abnormal ECG (Abnormal EKG): What It Means on Your Report](https://www.ecgmeans.com/abnormal-ecg/): Abnormal ECG or abnormal EKG on your report? What it means, what an abnormal EKG looks like, harmless vs serious causes, anxiety, and what happens next.
- [Anterior Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/anterior-infarct-age-undetermined/): What 'anterior infarct, age undetermined' or 'possible anterior infarct' means on an ECG printout, why it is often a false alarm, and which test settles it.
- [Anteroseptal Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/anteroseptal-infarct/): 'Anteroseptal infarct, age undetermined' means Q waves or lost R waves in V1–V4. Why lead placement often mimics it, and what confirms it.
- [Artifact on an ECG: What It Means When Your Report Mentions It](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-artifact/): Artifact on an ECG is electrical "noise" from movement, tremor or equipment, not the heart. Learn the types, how it can mimic VT or AFib, and what to do next.
- [Biatrial Enlargement on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/biatrial-enlargement/): Biatrial enlargement on an ECG means signs that both upper heart chambers are enlarged or strained. It needs a check-up, but it is not an emergency on its own.
- [Borderline ECG: What It Means and When to Worry](https://www.ecgmeans.com/borderline-ecg/): Borderline ECG meaning explained: what a borderline ECG result is, the small findings that cause it, why it is usually harmless, and when it needs follow-up.
- [Brugada Pattern on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/brugada-syndrome/): Brugada pattern on ECG means a possible inherited sodium channel condition. Learn what it looks like, what triggers it, and why it needs specialist review.
- [Cardiac Tamponade on an ECG: The Signs and Why It Is an Emergency](https://www.ecgmeans.com/cardiac-tamponade-ecg/): Cardiac tamponade on an ECG shows sinus tachycardia, low voltage QRS and electrical alternans. What the triad means, Beck's triad, and why it is an emergency.
- [Digoxin Effect on an ECG: What It Means and How It Differs From Toxicity](https://www.ecgmeans.com/digoxin-effect-ecg/): Digoxin effect on an ECG is a scooped "reverse tick" ST dip from the drug itself. How it differs from digoxin toxicity ECG signs, symptoms and blood levels.
- [Early Repolarization on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/early-repolarization/): Early repolarization is a common ECG variant in young, fit people. Learn what it looks like, why it is usually benign, and the rare situations where it matters.
- [Heart Palpitations but a Normal ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/heart-palpitations-normal-ecg/): Heart palpitations but a normal ECG? Why a 10-second test often misses them, common harmless causes like anxiety and PVCs, which monitors help, and red flags.
- [Hyperkalemia on an ECG: What the Changes Mean](https://www.ecgmeans.com/hyperkalemia-ecg/): Hyperkalemia ECG changes in order: peaked T waves, flat P waves, wide QRS, sine wave ECG. Potassium-level table, why the ECG can mislead, and urgent steps.
- [Hypokalaemia on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/hypokalemia-ecg/): Hypokalaemia on an ECG means low blood potassium, shown by flat T waves and U waves. Learn what it means, why it needs clinician review, and what happens next.
- [Inferior Infarct, Age Undetermined: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/inferior-infarct-age-undetermined/): 'Inferior infarct, age undetermined' means Q waves in II, III and aVF that can follow an old heart attack. Learn why it is often a false alarm.
- [Lateral Infarct: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/lateral-infarct/): A lateral infarct means Q waves or changes in leads I, aVL, V5–V6. What it suggests about the heart's side wall and how it is confirmed.
- [Left Axis Deviation: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-axis-deviation/): Left axis deviation on an ECG means the heart's electrical axis points left of −30°. What the numbers mean, common causes and when it needs more checking.
- [Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH): What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-ventricular-hypertrophy/): 'Possible left ventricular hypertrophy' (LVH) on an ECG means tall QRS complexes. Why the ECG over-calls it and which test confirms it.
- [Low Voltage QRS: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/low-voltage-qrs/): Low voltage QRS means the main spikes on your ECG are smaller than usual. Learn the criteria, harmless and important causes, and the usual next tests.
- [Nonspecific ST Abnormality on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/nonspecific-st-abnormality/): Nonspecific ST abnormality means small ST or T wave changes that don't point to a specific diagnosis. Usually benign, but context and old ECGs matter.
- [Nonspecific T Wave Abnormality: What It Means and Whether to Worry](https://www.ecgmeans.com/nonspecific-t-wave-abnormality/): Nonspecific T wave abnormality means flat or slightly inverted T waves without a disease pattern. Causes, the inferior-lead variant, when to worry.
- [P Mitrale on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/p-mitrale/): P mitrale is a broad, notched P wave on an ECG that suggests left atrial enlargement. Learn what causes it, whether to worry, and what usually happens next.
- [P Pulmonale on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/p-pulmonale/): P pulmonale means a tall, peaked P wave on your ECG, a sign of right atrial enlargement often linked to lung disease. Learn what it means and when to worry.
- [Pericarditis on an ECG: Stages, Signs and How It Differs From a Heart Attack](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pericarditis-ecg/): Pericarditis ECG: widespread concave ST elevation and PR depression. See the 4 stages and how it differs from STEMI and early repolarization on the EKG.
- [Poor R Wave Progression: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/poor-r-wave-progression/): Poor R wave progression (PRWP) on an ECG means R waves fail to grow across V1–V4. It is often lead position or body build, sometimes an old heart attack.
- [Possible Left Atrial Enlargement: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-atrial-enlargement/): 'Possible left atrial enlargement' is based on your P wave shape. How reliable it is, what enlarges the left atrium, and why an echo decides.
- [Possible Right Atrial Enlargement: ECG Meaning](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-atrial-enlargement/): 'Possible right atrial enlargement' is read from a tall, peaked P wave (P pulmonale). Learn what causes it and why an echocardiogram is the real test.
- [Posterior MI: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/posterior-mi/): A posterior MI is a heart attack affecting the back of the heart, shown by ST depression and tall R waves in V1–V3. Learn what it means and why it is urgent.
- [Pulmonary Embolism on an ECG: What It Shows](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pulmonary-embolism-ecg/): A pulmonary embolism can cause ECG changes like sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 and right heart strain. Learn why a normal ECG still can't rule it out.
- [Right Axis Deviation: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-axis-deviation/): Right axis deviation means the heart's electrical direction points further right than normal. See the causes, when it is a normal variant, and when it matters.
- [Right Heart Strain: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-heart-strain/): Right heart strain means the right ventricle is working against high pressure, shown by T-wave inversion in V1–V3 and other signs. Learn what it means.
- [Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-ventricular-hypertrophy/): Right ventricular hypertrophy on an ECG shows a tall R in V1 and right axis deviation. What thickens the right ventricle and how echo confirms it.
- [Septal Infarct on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/septal-infarct/): 'Septal infarct, age undetermined' is one of the commonest ECG false alarms. What the machine saw, why it is often wrong, and how it is checked.
- [Sgarbossa Criteria: Finding a Heart Attack in LBBB](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sgarbossa-criteria/): The Sgarbossa criteria help detect a heart attack when the ECG already shows a left bundle branch block or a paced rhythm. Learn what the three signs mean.
- [Tombstone ECG: What "Tombstoning" Means on an EKG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/tombstone-ecg/): A tombstone ECG shows huge dome-shaped ST elevation merging with the T wave, usually a large anterior STEMI from a blocked LAD. Meaning and why it's urgent.
- [Wellens Syndrome: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/wellens-syndrome/): Wellens syndrome is a pattern of T-wave changes in V2–V3 that warns of a critically narrowed LAD artery. Learn what the ECG signs mean and why it is urgent.

## Heart Rhythms
- [Heart Rhythms on the ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/heart-rhythms/): Heart rhythms on the ECG explained: sinus rhythm, AFib, flutter, SVT, junctional and ventricular rhythms, PVCs, bigeminy and trigeminy, and when each matters.
- [Accelerated Idioventricular Rhythm (AIVR) on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/accelerated-idioventricular-rhythm/): Accelerated idioventricular rhythm (AIVR) is a rhythm from the heart's lower chambers, often benign after a blocked artery reopens. Here's when to worry.
- [Accelerated Junctional Rhythm: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/accelerated-junctional-rhythm/): Accelerated junctional rhythm is a narrow-QRS rhythm from the AV junction at 60–100 bpm. See ECG criteria, causes like digoxin, risks and how it is treated.
- [AFib With RVR: What It Means on an ECG and How It Is Treated](https://www.ecgmeans.com/afib-with-rvr/): AFib with RVR is atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, a fast irregular heartbeat. What AFib RVR means, ECG signs, causes and treatment.
- [Ashman Phenomenon: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ashman-phenomenon/): Ashman phenomenon is a wide beat caused by aberrant conduction after a change in rhythm, often in atrial fibrillation. Learn what it means and why it is benign.
- [Asystole on an ECG: What a Flatline Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/asystole/): Asystole on an ECG is a flatline with no electrical activity: cardiac arrest. How it's confirmed, why it isn't shocked, CPR and epinephrine, and outlook.
- [Atrial Bigeminy: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-bigeminy/): Atrial bigeminy means every normal beat is followed by an early atrial beat (a PAC). Learn what it means, its causes and why it is usually harmless.
- [Atrial Fibrillation ECG: What AFib Looks Like and What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-fibrillation/): Atrial fibrillation ECG explained: what AFib looks like on an EKG strip, key criteria (no P waves, irregular RR), rate types, look-alikes and when to worry.
- [Atrial Flutter ECG: What the Sawtooth Pattern Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-flutter/): Atrial flutter ECG explained: sawtooth flutter waves, 2:1 conduction at about 150 bpm, other block ratios, how it differs from AFib on an EKG, next steps.
- [Atrial Tachycardia: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/atrial-tachycardia/): Atrial tachycardia is a fast rhythm from a focus in the atria, with abnormal P waves before each beat. Learn how it differs from sinus tachycardia and SVT.
- [AV Dissociation: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/av-dissociation/): AV dissociation means the atria and ventricles are beating independently. Learn what it means on an ECG, the causes, and why context decides if it matters.
- [AVNRT on an ECG: What AV Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/avnrt/): AVNRT is the most common SVT. How it looks on an ECG (pseudo-r' in V1), why it happens, vagal maneuvers, adenosine, ablation, and how it differs from AVRT.
- [Bigeminy (PVC Bigeminy): What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/bigeminy/): Bigeminy PVCs mean every other heartbeat is an early extra beat. How a bigeminy ECG looks, ventricular vs atrial bigeminy, causes, and when to get checked.
- [ECG Rhythm Strips: A Visual Library of EKG Rhythms](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-rhythm-strips/): Visual library of 36 ECG rhythm strips — sinus, atrial, junctional, ventricular and heart blocks — with rate, P waves, QRS and the key clue.
- [Ectopic Atrial Rhythm: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ectopic-atrial-rhythm/): An ectopic atrial rhythm starts outside the sinus node, so the P waves look unusual. Learn why it is often a benign variant and when it needs checking.
- [Ectopic Beats on an ECG: What They Mean](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ectopic-heartbeat/): Ectopic beats are extra, early heartbeats that start outside the sinus node. Very common and usually harmless. Learn what they mean and when to get checked.
- [Fusion Beat: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/fusion-beat/): A fusion beat forms when a normal beat and a ventricular beat activate the heart together, making a hybrid shape. Learn what a fusion beat means on an ECG.
- [Idioventricular Rhythm: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/idioventricular-rhythm/): Idioventricular rhythm is a slow, wide-complex back-up rhythm from the ventricles. Learn the rates, how AIVR differs, and why context decides how serious it is.
- [Junctional Bradycardia: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-bradycardia/): Junctional bradycardia is a slow heart rhythm from the AV junction, often under 40 beats per minute. Learn what it means, common causes and when it matters.
- [Junctional Escape Rhythm on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-escape-rhythm/): A junctional escape rhythm is a backup heart rhythm from the AV junction. It's usually protective; what matters is why the sinus node stopped leading.
- [Junctional Rhythm on an ECG: What It Means, Types and Rates](https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-rhythm/): Junctional rhythm on an ECG: the AV junction paces the heart at 40–60 bpm. Learn the ECG criteria, escape vs accelerated vs tachycardia, causes and treatment.
- [Junctional Tachycardia: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/junctional-tachycardia/): Junctional tachycardia is a fast rhythm from the AV junction, over 100 bpm, with absent or inverted P waves. Learn the ECG signs, causes, risks and treatment.
- [Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia (MAT): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/multifocal-atrial-tachycardia/): Multifocal atrial tachycardia is a fast, irregular rhythm with three or more P wave shapes, linked to lung disease. Learn how it differs from AFib.
- [Multifocal PVCs: What They Mean on Your ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/multifocal-pvcs/): Multifocal PVCs are extra beats of 2+ shapes from different spots in the ventricles. How they differ from unifocal PVCs, causes, tests and when to worry.
- [Normal Sinus Rhythm: What Sinus Rhythm Means on Your ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-rhythm/): Normal sinus rhythm is the heart's healthy rhythm at 60–100 bpm. What sinus rhythm means on an ECG, the NSR criteria, and what added report words mean.
- [Paced Rhythm on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/paced-rhythm/): A paced rhythm on your ECG means your pacemaker is producing some or all heartbeats. Learn what it looks like and when it needs a closer look.
- [Premature Junctional Contraction on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/premature-junctional-contraction/): A premature junctional contraction (PJC) is an early extra beat from the heart's AV junction. It's usually harmless and doesn't need treatment. Here's why.
- [Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA): What It Looks Like on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pulseless-electrical-activity/): What does PEA look like on an ECG? Pulseless electrical activity shows an organized rhythm but no pulse. Causes (Hs and Ts), treatment and outlook.
- [PVCs of the Heart (Premature Ventricular Contractions): What They Mean](https://www.ecgmeans.com/premature-ventricular-contractions/): PVCs are early extra heartbeats from the lower chambers. What a PVC looks like on an ECG, are PVCs dangerous, what PVC burden % means, and when to get help.
- [R-on-T Phenomenon: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/r-on-t-phenomenon/): R-on-T phenomenon means a premature beat lands on the previous T wave, during the heart's vulnerable period. Learn what it means and why it can matter.
- [Sick Sinus Syndrome on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sick-sinus-syndrome/): Sick sinus syndrome means the heart's natural pacemaker no longer keeps a reliable rate. It needs clinician review, mainly if it causes dizziness or fainting.
- [Sinus Bradycardia: What It Means on Your ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-bradycardia/): Sinus bradycardia on an ECG or EKG is a normal rhythm under 60 bpm. Why it is common in fit people and sleep, its causes, and which symptoms need attention.
- [Sinus Pause and Sinus Arrest: What They Mean](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-pause-arrest/): A sinus pause is a gap where the heart's pacemaker briefly stops firing. Learn how long is significant, the common causes, and when a pause needs a pacemaker.
- [Sinus Rhythm With PACs: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-rhythm-with-pac/): Sinus rhythm with PACs means a normal ECG/EKG rhythm with occasional early beats from the upper chambers. How PACs look, causes, and when to follow up.
- [Sinus Rhythm With Sinus Arrhythmia: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-arrhythmia/): Sinus arrhythmia on an ECG or EKG is usually a normal speeding and slowing of the heart with breathing. What it means, ECG criteria, and when it needs a look.
- [Sinus Tachycardia: What It Means, Causes and Treatment](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinus-tachycardia/): Sinus tachycardia is a normal rhythm over 100 bpm, usually the heart responding to something. Causes, treatment, inappropriate sinus tachycardia and POTS.
- [SVT on an ECG: What Supraventricular Tachycardia Looks Like and Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/supraventricular-tachycardia/): SVT on an ECG is a fast, regular, narrow-QRS rhythm at 150–250 bpm. What SVT looks like on an ECG strip, AVNRT vs AVRT vs atrial tachycardia, and next steps.
- [Torsades de Pointes: The "Twisting" Polymorphic VT on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/torsades-de-pointes/): Torsades de pointes is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with twisting QRS on the ECG, tied to long QT. Causes, magnesium treatment and prevention.
- [Trigeminy: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/trigeminy/): Trigeminy means every third heartbeat on your ECG is an extra beat. Learn what ventricular and atrial trigeminy look like, the causes, risks and treatment.
- [Ventricular Bigeminy: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-bigeminy/): Ventricular bigeminy means every normal beat is followed by a PVC (an extra ventricular beat). Learn what it means, common causes and when it matters.
- [Ventricular Couplet: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-couplet/): A ventricular couplet is two premature ventricular beats (PVCs) in a row. Learn what a couplet means on an ECG, common causes and when it needs attention.
- [Ventricular Fibrillation on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-fibrillation/): Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a chaotic heart rhythm that stops the heart pumping. It is a cardiac arrest and needs immediate CPR and defibrillation.
- [Ventricular Tachycardia on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-tachycardia/): Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a fast, wide-QRS rhythm from the heart's lower chambers. It can be life-threatening and is treated as an emergency.
- [Ventricular Trigeminy: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ventricular-trigeminy/): Ventricular trigeminy means every third beat is a PVC — two normal beats then an early ventricular beat. Learn what it means, causes and when it matters.
- [Wandering Atrial Pacemaker: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/wandering-atrial-pacemaker/): Wandering atrial pacemaker (WAP) on an ECG or EKG means the beat's starting point shifts, so P waves change shape. Usually benign; how it differs from MAT.
- [What Is a Dangerous Heart Rate With AFib?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/afib-heart-rate/): What is a dangerous heart rate with AFib? Target AFib heart rate ranges, when a fast (RVR) or slow rate is an emergency, and how to measure your pulse.

## Heart Blocks & Conduction
- [Types of Heart Block: AV Blocks and Bundle Branch Blocks](https://www.ecgmeans.com/heart-block-conduction/): Types of heart block explained: first, second and third degree AV block, bundle branch and fascicular blocks, with ECG signs and which ones are serious.
- [2:1 AV Block: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/2-1-av-block/): In 2:1 AV block every other P wave is blocked. It can be the benign Mobitz I type or the more serious Mobitz II type. Learn how doctors tell them apart.
- [Bifascicular Block: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/bifascicular-block/): Bifascicular block on an ECG means two of the heart's three wiring branches are blocked, usually RBBB plus LAFB. Its causes, risk and when a pacemaker helps.
- [Incomplete Left Bundle Branch Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/incomplete-left-bundle-branch-block/): Incomplete left bundle branch block is a partial delay in the heart's left conduction branch, with a QRS not yet fully widened. Learn what it means on an ECG.
- [Incomplete Right Bundle Branch Block on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/incomplete-right-bundle-branch-block/): Incomplete right bundle branch block (IRBBB) is a mild, partial delay in the heart's right-side wiring. Usually harmless—here's what it means and when to check.
- [Intraventricular Conduction Delay (IVCD): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/intraventricular-conduction-delay/): A nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay is a wide QRS that is not a typical bundle branch block. Learn the common causes and when it needs assessment.
- [LBBB on an ECG: What Left Bundle Branch Block Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-bundle-branch-block/): LBBB ECG explained: the left side of the heart's wiring is delayed. Criteria, causes, what a new LBBB means, and left bundle branch block life expectancy.
- [Left Anterior Fascicular Block (LAFB): What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-anterior-fascicular-block/): Left anterior fascicular block (LAFB, left anterior hemiblock) is a minor wiring delay that shifts the ECG axis left. Causes, criteria and when it matters.
- [Left Posterior Fascicular Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/left-posterior-fascicular-block/): Left posterior fascicular block is an uncommon conduction delay causing right axis deviation. Because the fascicle is sturdy, it often signals real disease.
- [Lown-Ganong-Levine (LGL) Syndrome](https://www.ecgmeans.com/lown-ganong-levine-syndrome/): Lown-Ganong-Levine (LGL) syndrome is a short PR interval with a normal QRS plus episodes of fast heartbeat. Learn what this pre-excitation pattern means.
- [Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB): What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/right-bundle-branch-block/): Right bundle branch block (RBBB) on an ECG means the right ventricle fires slightly late. What complete and incomplete RBBB mean, causes and when to worry.
- [Second Degree AV Block Type 1 (Mobitz I / Wenckebach): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/second-degree-av-block-type-1/): Second degree AV block type 1 (Mobitz I, Wenckebach heart block): how it looks on an ECG, why it is usually benign, and how it differs from Mobitz II.
- [Second Degree AV Block Type 2 (Mobitz II): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/second-degree-av-block-type-2/): Second degree AV block type 2 (Mobitz type 2) drops beats suddenly with a constant PR. ECG signs, type 1 vs type 2, symptoms, and why a pacemaker helps.
- [Sinoatrial (SA) Block on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/sinoatrial-block/): SA block means the sinus node fires but its signal is delayed or blocked, causing a missed beat. Often harmless; it matters if pauses cause symptoms.
- [Sinus Rhythm With 1st Degree AV Block: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/first-degree-av-block/): First degree AV block means the atria-to-ventricles signal is slightly delayed (PR over 200 ms). Why it is usually benign and when it matters.
- [Third Degree AV Block (Complete Heart Block): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/third-degree-av-block/): Third degree AV block (complete heart block) means no signals reach the ventricles. How it looks on an ECG, symptoms, causes, and why a pacemaker is needed.
- [Trifascicular Block: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/trifascicular-block/): Trifascicular block means disease affecting all three conduction fascicles, often shown as bifascicular block plus a prolonged PR. Learn what it means.
- [Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW): What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/wolff-parkinson-white/): Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) is an extra electrical pathway that shows as a short PR and a delta wave on the ECG. Learn what WPW means and when it matters.

## Intervals & Waves
- [ECG Intervals and Waves: Normal Ranges](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-intervals-waves/): ECG intervals and waves explained: normal PR, QRS and QT/QTc ranges, what short or long values mean, plus T wave, ST segment, Q wave and U wave changes.
- [Aberrant Conduction on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/aberrant-conduction/): Aberrant conduction means a beat from above took an unusual path through the ventricles, looking wide. It's usually benign but needs telling apart from VT.
- [Biphasic T Wave: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/biphasic-t-wave/): A biphasic T wave goes both up and down. Depending on the pattern it can mean low potassium, ischaemia (Wellens), or be a minor finding. Learn how it is read.
- [De Winter T Waves: What They Mean on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/de-winter-t-waves/): De Winter T waves are upsloping ST depression with tall T waves in V1–V6 that signal a blocked LAD artery. Learn what this STEMI-equivalent pattern means.
- [Delta Wave: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/delta-wave/): A delta wave is a slurred upstroke at the start of the QRS, the signature of Wolff-Parkinson-White. Learn what it means, the risks, and when it needs treatment.
- [Electrical Alternans: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/electrical-alternans/): Electrical alternans is a beat-to-beat change in QRS height on an ECG. Learn why fluid around the heart is the classic cause and when it is urgent.
- [Epsilon Wave: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/epsilon-wave/): An epsilon wave is a small deflection after the QRS, best known as a sign of ARVC. Learn what an epsilon wave means on an ECG and why it needs assessment.
- [Fragmented QRS: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/fragmented-qrs/): A fragmented QRS has extra notches or spikes from scarred heart muscle. Learn what fragmented QRS means on an ECG, its causes and why it can be a useful marker.
- [Hyperacute T Waves: What They Mean on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/hyperacute-t-waves/): Hyperacute T waves are tall, broad T waves that can be the earliest sign of a heart attack. Learn what they mean on an ECG and why they need urgent attention.
- [Inverted P Wave on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/inverted-p-wave/): An inverted P wave on ECG means the atria were activated in an unusual direction. Often harmless, such as swapped leads. See what it means and when to worry.
- [J-Point Elevation on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/j-point-elevation/): J-point elevation means the end of the QRS sits just above baseline. In young, healthy people it's usually benign early repolarisation. See when it matters.
- [Normal PR Interval: Normal Range, How to Measure It, and Short or Prolonged PR](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pr-interval/): A normal PR interval is 120–200 ms (3–5 small boxes). How to measure the PR interval, the normal range by age, and what a prolonged or short PR means.
- [Normal QT Interval: QT and QTc Normal Range Explained](https://www.ecgmeans.com/qt-interval/): Normal QT interval and QTc normal range by sex and age, how the QT is measured and corrected for heart rate, what a long or short QTc means, when to worry.
- [Osborn Wave (J Wave): What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/osborn-wave/): An Osborn wave (J wave) is a notch at the end of the QRS, classically from hypothermia. What it looks like, its causes, and why it fades on warming.
- [Pathological Q Waves: What They Mean on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pathological-q-waves/): Pathological Q waves are deep or wide Q waves that often signal a past heart attack. Learn what they mean on an ECG, how they differ from normal Q waves.
- [Peaked T Waves: What They Mean on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/peaked-t-waves/): Tall, peaked T waves can be a normal variant or an early warning of high potassium. Learn how to tell them apart and why new peaked T waves need prompt testing.
- [QRS Interval: Normal QRS Duration and What a Wide QRS Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/qrs-interval/): QRS interval explained: normal QRS duration (under 120 ms, usually 70–110), how to measure it, what 110–119 ms or a wide QRS of 120 ms+ means, and causes.
- [QT Prolongation on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/qt-prolongation/): QT prolongation on an ECG means the heart takes longer than normal to reset between beats. Learn what QTc numbers mean, common causes and when to worry.
- [S1Q3T3: What the Pattern Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/s1q3t3/): S1Q3T3 is an ECG pattern linked with pulmonary embolism, but it is neither sensitive nor specific. What it is, why it happens, how PE is diagnosed.
- [Short PR Interval on an ECG: Causes, Meaning and When It Matters](https://www.ecgmeans.com/short-pr-interval/): A short PR interval (under 120 ms) is usually a harmless fast-conduction variant. Causes, what it means, when it points to WPW, and next steps.
- [ST Depression: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/st-depression/): ST depression means the ST segment sits below the baseline. It can signal reduced blood flow to the heart, or be caused by strain, digoxin or a fast heart rate.
- [ST Elevation: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/st-elevation/): ST elevation can signal a heart attack (STEMI) but also has harmless causes like early repolarization and pericarditis. Learn what separates them.
- [T Wave Inversion: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/t-wave-inversion/): Inverted T waves can be normal in some leads and important in others. Learn where T wave inversion is expected, which patterns matter, and how it is assessed.
- [U Wave: What It Means on an ECG](https://www.ecgmeans.com/u-wave/): A U wave is a small bump after the T wave. Small U waves are normal; prominent U waves can signal low potassium or certain medicines. Learn when it matters.
- [What Does the P Wave Represent on an ECG?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/p-wave/): What does the P wave represent on an ECG? Atrial depolarization. Normal P wave values, plus what P mitrale, P pulmonale, inverted or absent P waves mean.
- [Wide QRS Complex on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/wide-qrs-complex/): A wide QRS complex means the heart's ventricles took longer than normal to activate. Learn what causes it and when it matters, as it depends on context.

## Comparisons
- [ECG Comparisons: This vs That](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-comparisons/): ECG comparisons in plain English: PVC vs PAC, SVT vs VT, AFib vs flutter, LBBB vs RBBB, STEMI vs NSTEMI and EKG vs echo, with which one needs more attention.
- [AFib vs VFib: What Is the Difference?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/afib-vs-vfib/): AFib vs VFib: atrial vs ventricular fibrillation compared — ECG signs, symptoms, pulse and consciousness, and why VFib needs CPR and defibrillation at once.
- [Atrial Fibrillation vs Atrial Flutter on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/afib-vs-aflutter/): Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter are related fast heart rhythms that look different on an ECG. Learn how they differ, their stroke risk and treatment.
- [ECG vs EKG: What's the Difference?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-vs-ekg/): ECG vs EKG: they are the same heart test. Why EKG has a K, what EKG stands for, what it shows, its types, and how it differs from an EEG and an echo.
- [Echocardiogram vs EKG: What's the Difference and Do You Need Both?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ekg-vs-echocardiogram/): Echocardiogram vs EKG: an EKG records the heart's electrical signals; an echo is an ultrasound of structure. Is an echo the same as an EKG? Key differences.
- [EEG vs EKG: What Is the Difference Between These Two Tests?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/eeg-vs-ekg/): EEG vs EKG compared: an EEG records brain waves, an EKG records the heart's electrical activity. Electrodes, test time, what each finds, and how to prepare.
- [Left vs Right Bundle Branch Block on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/lbbb-vs-rbbb/): Left and right bundle branch block both widen the QRS on an ECG. Learn how they differ, why RBBB is often benign, and when LBBB needs more checks.
- [NSTEMI vs STEMI on an ECG: What the Difference Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/stemi-vs-nstemi/): NSTEMI ECG changes vs STEMI: what an NSTEMI EKG shows (ST depression, T inversion or near-normal), why troponin confirms it, and why both are emergencies.
- [PAC vs PVC: What's the Difference on an ECG?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/pvc-vs-pac/): PAC vs PVC on ECG: a side-by-side guide to P waves, QRS width and pauses, causes, symptoms, PVC burden percentages, and when follow-up is needed.
- [SVT vs VTach: What's the Difference?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/svt-vs-vtach/): SVT vs ventricular tachycardia: both are fast rhythms but differ in origin, ECG look and danger. How doctors tell them apart and treat each.

## ECG Basics
- [ECG Basics for Patients](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-basics/): ECG basics for patients: what an EKG is, how leads are placed, how to read your ECG report, what a normal ECG can and cannot rule out, and what to ask.
- [12 Lead ECG Placement: Where Every Electrode Goes and Why](https://www.ecgmeans.com/12-lead-ecg-placement/): 12 lead ECG placement step by step: limb electrodes, exact V1–V6 landmarks, women, posterior V7–V9, V4R, and how misplaced leads change the tracing.
- [3 Lead ECG Placement and the Einthoven Triangle](https://www.ecgmeans.com/3-lead-ecg-placement/): 3 lead ECG placement explained: where the three electrodes go, AHA and IEC colors, why lead II is used for monitoring, 4-lead setups, and key limits.
- [5 Lead ECG Placement and ECG Leads Explained](https://www.ecgmeans.com/5-lead-ecg-placement/): 5 lead ECG placement made simple: where each electrode goes, AHA and IEC color codes, the "white on right" mnemonic, and what ECG leads actually are.
- [Can an EKG Detect a Heart Attack? What It Shows and What It Can Miss](https://www.ecgmeans.com/can-an-ekg-detect-a-heart-attack/): Can an EKG detect a heart attack? Often, not always. What a heart attack looks like on an EKG, STEMI vs NSTEMI, old heart attacks, and why troponin matters.
- [Does an EKG Show Blockage in Your Heart Arteries?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/does-an-ekg-show-blockage/): Does an EKG show blockage in the heart arteries? Usually not at rest. Learn what clues it can give, how "heart block" differs, and which tests find blockages.
- [EKG Interpretation Cheat Sheet (ECG Quick Reference)](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-interpretation-cheat-sheet/): EKG interpretation cheat sheet: normal values, rate table, rhythm and heart block recognition, axis rules, STEMI territories, electrolytes and mnemonics.
- [How to Read an EKG Strip: A Simple 8-Step Method](https://www.ecgmeans.com/how-to-read-an-ekg-strip/): How to read an EKG strip in 8 steps: paper and boxes, rate, rhythm, P waves, PR, QRS, QTc and ST-T, plus a worked example. EKG for dummies, made simple.
- [How to Read Your ECG Report: A Plain-English Guide](https://www.ecgmeans.com/how-to-read-ecg-report/): A step-by-step guide to the numbers and phrases printed on a 12-lead ECG report — rate, PR, QRS, QT/QTc, axis, the machine's findings and its overall verdict.
- [If My ECG Is Normal, Is My Heart OK?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/if-ecg-is-normal-is-my-heart-ok/): A normal ECG or EKG is reassuring for rhythm and acute damage but can't rule out all heart problems. What it shows, what it misses, and which tests come next.
- [Wandering Baseline on an ECG: What It Means](https://www.ecgmeans.com/wandering-baseline-ecg/): Wandering baseline on an ECG is a recording artifact, not a heart problem. Learn what causes the drift, why it's harmless and why the ECG may be repeated.
- [What Can an EKG Detect? What It Finds, What It Hints At, and What It Misses](https://www.ecgmeans.com/what-can-an-ekg-detect/): What can an EKG detect? A clear table of what it finds well, what it only hints at (like heart failure and valve disease), and what it cannot show at all.
- [What Is an EKG (ECG), and How Long Does an EKG Take?](https://www.ecgmeans.com/what-is-an-ekg/): What an EKG is, what it measures and how long an EKG takes (usually 5–10 minutes). How it is done, what to wear, when results come, and what EKG stands for.
- [Where to Get an EKG and How Much It Costs](https://www.ecgmeans.com/where-to-get-an-ekg/): How much does an EKG cost with or without insurance? Does urgent care do EKGs? Where to get one, typical US price ranges, Medicare coverage, what to expect.

## ECG Tools & Calculators
- [ECG Tools and Calculators](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-tools/): Free ECG calculators: QTc calculator, heart rate from an ECG strip, QRS axis calculator and a normal ECG values chart, with plain-English guides to each.
- [ECG Axis Calculator](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-axis-calculator/): Free ECG axis calculator. Enter the net QRS size in leads I and aVF to get the electrical axis in degrees and see if it is normal, left or right axis deviation.
- [EKG Practice Strips: Interactive Rhythm Quiz](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ekg-practice-strips/): Free EKG practice strips quiz: identify 36 ECG rhythms, from sinus rhythm to VFib and heart blocks, with instant answers and the key clue for every strip.
- [How to Calculate Heart Rate on an ECG: 6 Second, 300 and 1500 Methods](https://www.ecgmeans.com/ecg-heart-rate-calculator/): Use the 6 second ECG method, the 300 rule or the 1500 rule to calculate heart rate on an ECG. Free calculator, worked examples and normal heart rates by age.
- [Normal EKG Results: Normal ECG Values and Intervals (Adults)](https://www.ecgmeans.com/normal-ecg-values/): Normal EKG results explained: what a normal EKG looks like, a normal ECG values chart (rate, PR, QRS, QTc, axis) and what out-of-range values mean.
- [QTc Calculator (Corrected QT Interval)](https://www.ecgmeans.com/qtc-calculator/): Free QTc calculator. Enter the QT interval and heart rate to get the corrected QT by Bazett, Fridericia, Framingham and Hodges, with normal ranges explained.
